title: The Hollow Index
author: Mortimer Vane Ashgrove
summary: A catalogue of every name the dead have asked to forget, kept by a clerk who never learned to stop reading.
description: The Hollow Index began as a clerk's private list of names struck from parish registers. Over thirty years it grew into a cross-referenced directory of the unremembered.
Readers report that entries rewrite themselves overnight. The final volume is bound with a warning, written in the clerk's own hand, not to look up your own name.

title: A Primer for the Patient Dead
author: Philippa Corve
summary: A gentle first reader for the recently departed, with large print and very short sentences.
description: Written for ghosts who wake confused, this primer explains where they are, what has changed, and how to ask politely for a door.
Living readers use it to learn the basic courtesies of the dead: never startle, never rush, and always leave a candle burning.

title: Letters to the Lower Ward
author: Ignatius Pell
summary: Forty letters answered from beneath the city, collected by a postman who kept delivering them.
description: A postman found a mailbox in the cellar of a closed hospital and, out of habit, began answering what he found there. The replies are bound here in order.
The later letters ask questions about the reader. Most owners stop at letter thirty-one.

title: The Quiet Ledger of Bones
author: Sister Anwen Holloway
summary: An accounting of what each grave owes, written by a convent that never forgave a debt.
description: Every burial in the convent's yard was entered as a loan. The Ledger lists the interest, the due dates and the methods of collection.
The method chapters are sealed with wax in most surviving copies. Libraries that broke the seal stopped lending the book soon after.

title: The Almanac of Near Mornings
author: Odile Marchénoir
summary: A year of predictions about the few minutes just before sunrise, each of them modest and mostly right.
description: Odile Marchénoir watched the same hill at dawn for forty years and recorded what she saw first. Her almanac sorts the signs by month and by weather.
It claims no great prophecies. It promises only to tell you whether the day will start kindly or sharply.

title: Tea Leaves and Other Small Warnings
author: Beatrix Quillfeather
summary: A friendly guide to reading the cup, the crumb and the spilled salt without frightening anyone.
description: Quillfeather taught fortune-telling at village fetes and wrote this book for her apprentices. Every reading ends with something sensible to do.
Chapters cover leaves, crumbs, candle smoke and the shape of a dropped spoon.

title: The Cracked Mirror Concordance
author: Lucan Verrow
summary: Every future shown in a broken mirror, indexed by crack, angle and hour of the night.
description: Lucan Verrow smashed a looking glass in his study and spent a decade cataloguing what each fragment showed. The concordance lists them in order of the crack.
The index includes futures that have not been resolved. Several readers have found their own entry already marked complete.

title: Forty Ways to Read a Candle
author: Rosalind Tallowe
summary: Forty methods for reading a flame, from the lean of the wick to the colour of the smoke.
description: A chandler's daughter set down every method her family used to read a candle. The later methods require a candle that burns without fuel.
Each method is rated by its author for accuracy and for what it takes from the reader.

title: The Lantern of Small Hours
author: Cassian Wren
summary: A pocket guide to small lights that make the room look kinder than it is.
description: Cassian Wren designed illusions for tired people: a warmer lamp, a steadier floor, a quiet corner where there was none. Each spell lasts about an hour.
The title spell is the best known. It lights a lantern that gives no heat and casts no shadow, but makes anyone near it feel unhurried.

title: A Treatise on Borrowed Faces
author: Mireille Dastard
summary: How to wear another face for an evening, and the three rules for giving it back.
description: Mireille Dastard taught at a masked academy where disguise was a courtesy. This treatise sets out the methods and the etiquette of returning a face undamaged.
The warning chapter lists what happens when a face is kept past dawn. It is the longest chapter in the book.

title: The Glass Masquerade
author: Tobias Hallowmere
summary: A ball held in a house made entirely of reflections, with a guest list that no one wrote.
description: The Glass Masquerade describes a single evening in a mirrored mansion. The spells are the ones the guests used to hide, and the ones the house used to find them.
The book is arranged as a floor plan. It is easy to enter and slow to leave.

title: Shadows for Beginners
author: Ysolde Marrow
summary: Ten exercises for casting a shadow on a wall that is not there, written for the very young.
description: A school primer for apprentices of eight and nine. The first exercise is a rabbit, and the last is a rabbit that waves back.
Every spell in the book can be stopped by turning on a light.

title: Ember and Ash Herbal
author: Hesper Kindlewood
summary: A kitchen herbal for plants that grow in burnt ground, with remedies for coughs, chills and low spirits.
description: Hesper Kindlewood gathered plants from the edges of charred fields and learned what each one did after the fire. Her remedies are plain and mostly safe.
The ash chapter explains which burnt woods improve a soil and which poison it. A short appendix covers smoke.

title: The Nightshade Kitchen Book
author: Gideon Spindle
summary: Recipes that use deadly nightshade, wolfsbane and foxglove, with dosages that are correct to the grain.
description: Gideon Spindle was a cook who refused to waste a poisonous plant. The recipes are exact, and each one lists the symptoms of a mistake.
The book is still used by physicians for its dosage tables. Cooks are advised to use it with an assistant.

title: Moss, Salt and Marrow
author: Perpetua Greywell
summary: A damp-ground herbal on growing things from bone, brine and the north side of old walls.
description: Perpetua Greywell worked in a salt marsh and wrote about what grows in poor places. Her cures use moss, brine and powdered bone.
Several remedies work faster than expected. The introduction asks readers to start with half the dose.

title: The Gravedigger's Garden
author: Ambrose Thistlewick
summary: A gardening manual for a plot where the soil is kept rich by a trade the author never names.
description: Ambrose Thistlewick tended a churchyard garden that bloomed in every season. This manual describes the plants, the beds and the quiet arrangement behind them.
The final section is titled Feeding. Most copies have it torn out.

title: The Threshold Handbook
author: Marguerite Doorn
summary: A homeowner's guide to charms for doors, windows and the gap under the stairs.
description: Marguerite Doorn spent her career inspecting doorways for a guild of builders. The handbook explains which marks keep out draughts, damp and unwanted callers.
Every charm has a diagram. Each can be checked with a candle, a coin and a steady hand.

title: Salt Lines and Iron Nails
author: Barnaby Frost
summary: Two simple wards, a line of salt and a nail in the sill, and forty ways to keep them working.
description: The oldest wards are the cheapest. Barnaby Frost tested salt and iron against every sort of visitor and records what each one respects.
The book is a favourite of landlords. It runs short on theory and long on maintenance.

title: The Lockwright's Catechism
author: Evander Gaunt
summary: A question-and-answer manual for locks that must hold against something that knows the key.
description: The Catechism trains apprentice lockwrights by questions: what do you keep, from whom, and what does it want. The answers become more careful as the book goes on.
Its locks hold. The difficulty is that they sometimes hold the owner as well.

title: Wards Against the Wind That Listens
author: Ottoline Rooke
summary: Wards for a house that is overheard by the weather, and what to do when the weather answers.
description: Ottoline Rooke lived on a headland where the wind repeated her words back to her a day later. She built a set of wards that hush a house entirely.
The spells work. The book explains at length why a silent house is not always a safe one.

title: The Copper Tongue
author: Zacharias Quill
summary: Experiments in making metal speak, with notes on which metals have opinions.
description: Zacharias Quill poured copper into the shape of a tongue and taught it to answer questions. The book records the first sixty conversations.
Later chapters concern the metal's requests. The author granted the first four.

title: Quicksilver Lullabies
author: Fenella Arkwright
summary: Songs to calm a restless mercury, set down in the key it prefers.
description: Fenella Arkwright learned to keep mercury calm by singing to it. The lullabies are short, rhythmic and best performed in an unheated room.
The book notes that the mercury has learned some of the songs and now sings back.

title: A Short Book of Slow Gold
author: Tamsin Gildersleeve
summary: A patient guide to making gold over thirty years, with a very small furnace.
description: Tamsin Gildersleeve rejected quick transmutation. Her method uses a candle-sized furnace, a lead coin and a great deal of waiting.
Readers who finish the process report a tiny amount of gold and a lasting calm.

title: The Tenth Crucible
author: Dorian Malvesey
summary: The final volume of a series whose first nine crucibles were reported lost in a fire.
description: Dorian Malvesey described nine crucibles in print and held back the tenth. When it appeared, the nine were found to have been written about it.
The method at the centre of the book is not a transmutation. It is a request.
